children: Brokerage firm Jefferies says the surge in gold prices over the past year has created a hidden boost to India's economy, one that has not fully shown up yet. The firm laid out the numbers behind that view, along with stock picks tied to it.

Jefferies estimates Indian households hold about 25,000 tonnes of gold. It puts the value of this gold at $3.9 trillion as of March 2026, an increase of $1.9 trillion over just two years. That is about four times the value Indian households hold in stocks, and nearly 35 times the $111 billion in gold held by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).

Gold's share of total household wealth has also grown fast. Jefferies estimates gold made up 15.4% of Indian household assets in March 2023. By March 2026, that share had risen to 24.2%, even as total household assets grew from $11.3 trillion to $16.0 trillion. Over the same period, the share held in property fell from 51.3% to 47.6%, and the share held in bank deposits fell from 14.1% to 11.2%. Equities held roughly steady, at 5.6% and 5.7%.
Gold has also drawn money through exchange-traded funds. Jefferies said gold ETF assets rose from $2.8 billion in March 2023 to $18.1 billion in July 2026.
Gold loans have grown, but not as fast as prices

Gold is increasingly being used as loan collateral, not just held as savings. Jefferies estimates organised gold loan AUM (assets under management) stood at $197 billion as of March 2026, up 73% in dollar terms over the past two years. Gold loans now account for about 7% of total bank and NBFC credit in India, and gold-based lending has risen from under 4% of bank and NBFC credit before 2020 to about 5.1% in March 2026.

Even so, Jefferies says this growth has lagged behind the rise in gold prices. Gold loans as a share of the total value of household gold holdings actually fell by about 80 basis points from March 2024 levels, despite gold prices rising sharply over the same period. Jefferies estimates only around 15% of household gold is currently used as collateral, through formal or informal lending channels, assuming a loan-to-value ratio of about 65%.

The brokerage expects this gap to narrow. It estimates a "reversion" over the next two years could add 8 to 10 percentage points to the monetisation ratio, adding roughly $15-20 billion a year in gold loans. On top of that, Jefferies estimates a further 10% rise in gold prices could generate about $400 billion in additional household wealth and another $20-25 billion in gold loans. Together, Jefferies says this could add another 80 to 100 basis points of tailwind to GDP and consumer spending.
Why rural households matter here

Jefferies linked this specifically to weaker income growth in rural India. Unlike stock ownership, which is concentrated among wealthier and urban households, gold ownership is spread widely across rural and lower-income households. Jefferies said this makes the gold wealth effect a possible buffer for consumption at the bottom of the income pyramid, at a time of weak monsoon rains.
The cost: a bigger import bill

Rising gold prices are not only good news for India's economy, according to the note. Gold imports, including jewellery, are about 10% of India's total imports. Jefferies said this import bill rose from $36 billion in FY23 to $79 billion in FY26, equal to about 2% of GDP, and that this weighs on India's current account deficit (CAD). India's broader gems and jewellery market, which Jefferies estimates is about 80% gold jewellery, grew from $36 billion in FY19 to an estimated $118 billion in FY26.

Separately, RBI's own gold reserves have grown too, rising from $52 billion in March 2024 to $111 billion in August 2026. Gold's share of India's total foreign exchange reserves rose from about 8% to about 16% over roughly the same window.
The global backdrop

The note also cited Jefferies' global strategist Chris Wood, who has argued that fiscal pressures in the United States and Japan are supportive for gold prices. Jefferies pointed to US government data showing that net interest payments plus entitlement spending (social security, Medicare, health spending and veterans' benefits) reached 98.4% of total government receipts in the 12 months to July 2026, the highest level since June 2020. Wood's view, as cited in the note, is that this level of fiscal strain limits how much room central banks in the US and Japan have to raise interest rates, which is a positive backdrop for gold prices. Jefferies' base case is for gold prices to keep rising.
Stock picks

On stock picks, Jefferies named Manappuram Finance as its preferred way to play the gold loan trade. It added the stock to its India model portfolio with a Buy rating. Muthoot Finance, the other large listed gold financier discussed in the note, kept its Hold rating and was not added to the portfolio.

Jefferies also named other potential beneficiaries of higher gold prices that it did not add to the model portfolio, including jewellers Titan and Kalyan Jewellers, commodity exchange MCX, and lender IIFL Finance.

Along with Manappuram, Jefferies added Hindustan Zinc, Navin Fluorine and Meesho to its model portfolio. Hindustan Zinc was added partly for exposure to silver, alongside gold. Navin Fluorine was added on expected growth in its CDMO, cooling products, specialty chemicals and advanced materials businesses, where Jefferies expects 23% earnings per share growth a year between FY26 and FY29. Meesho was added as a play on mass discretionary consumption.
To fund these additions, Jefferies removed Ambuja Cements, Jindal Stainless and trimmed weight in select lenders including Bajaj Finance.

title: Rising gold prices could add up to 100 basis points to India's GDP: Jefferies
